title: Public Sector Workers Plan Strike Over Pay
summaryZh: 超過十萬名愛爾蘭公部門員工因薪資爭議，預計於10月14日罷工。
paragraphs: More than 100,000 public sector workers in Ireland are preparing to go on strike this Wednesday, 14 October, in a dispute over pay. Teachers, nurses, doctors and school support staff are all expected to take part, and further stoppages are planned for 21 October.

Several large trade unions are involved, including Fórsa, Siptu and the Irish Nurses and Midwives Organisation. For the first time, dentists working for the Health Service Executive (HSE) will also join the action.
The last public service pay agreement expired in June. The unions argue that wages have not kept up with inflation, and they accuse the Government of attaching conditions before talks can even begin.

The impact on daily life could be significant. Most schools may close, which means many working parents will have to take a day off or find someone to look after their children. In the health service, up to 150,000 medical appointments could be cancelled, although emergency care is expected to continue as normal.

The Minister for Public Expenditure, Jack Chambers, says an agreement could already have been reached. He claims the unions walked away after only two meetings, and he wants any new deal to include public service reform. In the recent budget, the Government set aside €1.2 billion for pay increases, but the unions say this is far from enough.
Experts in industrial relations believe a compromise is still possible. However, they warn that both sides need to act quickly if they want to avoid disruption next week.

More than 100,000 public sector employees across Ireland are poised to walk out this Wednesday, 14 October, in an escalating dispute over pay. Teachers, nurses, doctors and school support staff are all expected to participate, with further stoppages scheduled for 21 October.

A coalition of major trade unions is behind the action, among them Fórsa, Siptu and the Irish Nurses and Midwives Organisation. In a notable first, dentists employed by the Health Service Executive (HSE) will also take part.

The previous public service pay agreement lapsed in June. Union leaders contend that wages have failed to keep pace with inflation, and they accuse the Government of imposing preconditions before negotiations can even get under way.

The disruption to everyday life is likely to be considerable. Most schools are expected to close, leaving many working parents scrambling to arrange childcare or take leave. In the health service, as many as 150,000 appointments could be postponed, although emergency departments will continue to operate.

The Minister for Public Expenditure, Jack Chambers, insists that a settlement was within reach, claiming the unions abandoned talks after just two meetings. He is adamant that any new agreement must incorporate public service reform. The Government has earmarked €1.2 billion for pay increases in the latest budget, a figure the unions dismiss as wholly inadequate.
Industrial relations experts maintain that a compromise remains achievable, but warn that both sides must act decisively if next week's disruption is to be averted.

Over 100,000 public sector workers in Ireland are set to strike on Wednesday, 14 October, in a protracted dispute concerning remuneration. The industrial action will involve teachers, nurses, doctors and school support staff, and a second wave of stoppages has been scheduled for 21 October.

The action is being coordinated by several prominent trade unions, including Fórsa, Siptu and the Irish Nurses and Midwives Organisation. Significantly, dentists employed by the Health Service Executive (HSE) will participate in industrial action for the first time.

The most recent public service pay agreement expired in June. The unions argue that wage growth has lagged considerably behind inflation, thereby eroding workers' purchasing power, and they criticise the Government for stipulating conditions prior to formal negotiations.

The consequences for the wider public are expected to be substantial. The majority of schools are likely to close, obliging many working parents to take annual leave or seek alternative childcare. Within the health sector, up to 150,000 medical appointments may be cancelled, although emergency services will be maintained.

The Minister for Public Expenditure, Jack Chambers, contends that an agreement was attainable, asserting that the unions withdrew after merely two meetings. He maintains that any future settlement must be contingent on public service reform. Although the Government allocated €1.2 billion for pay increases in its most recent budget, the unions regard this sum as fundamentally insufficient.
Specialists in industrial relations consider a compromise feasible; nevertheless, they caution that prompt action from both parties is essential if further disruption is to be prevented.
